evidence_quotes.quote: This paper examines the impact of the recent MWSS privatization on the coverage and quality of water and sanitation services and ultimately on the groundwater levels, water pollution, human health, and welfare of the poor.

Analysis of the performance targets and other provisions of the MWSS concession agreement together with revised projections of water demand indicates that a significant share of water supply will have to be met through groundwater pumping

The progressive water price structure itself for MWSS water also ends up having regressive effects as the poorer households have to rely on shared water connection or public faucets and thereby pay higher water prices.

raw_response.plain_vs_narrow_note: No divergence between the plain and narrow readings of Criterion 2: the study directly examines specific utility-ownership/contractual rules (MWSS privatization and concession agreement performance targets and sewerage coverage exceptions) and tariff/pricing design rules (the progressive block tariff structure penalizing poor households reliant on shared connections or public faucets), satisfying both readings.
raw_response.rationale: This study clearly meets (or strongly appears to meet) all Phase 5 Title/Abstract inclusion criteria. C1 is satisfied because it focuses on urban household water supply and sewerage services in Metro Manila, including tap connections, shared connections and public faucets. C2 (both narrow and plain) is satisfied because it analyses MWSS utility privatization, specific provisions, performance targets and coverage exceptions in the MWSS concession agreement, and the progressive water tariff structure. C3 is satisfied at Title/Abstract stage because the paper conducts quantitative/socio-legal empirical and demand-projection analysis of service coverage, concession targets and water pricing (with full-text review to confirm the exact balance of primary empirical data versus demand projections). C4 is satisfied because it evaluates service coverage, water rationing/shortages and regressive affordability impacts on poor households paying higher prices via shared connections, public faucets and private water markets.
